summary: The Shaft size calculator turns the power transmitted (P) and the shaft rotation speed (N) into torque (T) (Power and torque). It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Shaft size calculator work?
sections.html:
The Shaft size calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports torque (T) (Power and torque) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (select design basis); then you type in the power transmitted (P) (Power and torque), the power transmitted (P) (Power and torque), the power transmitted (P) (Power and torque) and the shaft rotation speed (N) (Power and torque).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Shaft size calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Torque (T)=30 × power transmitted (P) ÷ (PI × shaft rotation speed (N))
Power transmitted (P)=(1 ÷ 30) × PI × torque (T) × shaft rotation speed (N)
Shaft rotation speed (N)=30 × power transmitted (P) ÷ (PI × torque (T))
Torque (T)=(1 ÷ 16) × PI × (diameter of solid shaft (d) ^ 3) × allowable shear stress (τ)
Torque (T)=(1 ÷ 16) × PI × (outer diameter of hollow shaft (dₒ) ^ 3) × allowable shear stress (τ) × (1 − (ratio of inner to outer diameter (k) ^ 4))
Outer diameter of hollow shaft (dₒ)=inner diameter of hollow shaft (dᵢ) ÷ ratio of inner to outer diameter (k)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Select design basis set to Twisting moment only, Power transmitted (P) = 10 kW and Shaft rotation speed (N) = 10 rpm. The calculator returns Torque (T) = 9.5493 N·m.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Torque (T) = 9.5493 N·m should be roughly the size you expected from Select design basis set to Twisting moment only and Power transmitted (P) = 10 kW.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Power, opening in kilowatts
  • Rotational speed, opening in rotations per minute
  • Torque, opening in newton meters
  • Power, opening in kilowatts
  • Rotational speed, opening in rotations per minute
  • Torque, opening in newton meters
  • Torque, opening in newton meters
  • Power, opening in kilowatts

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Shaft size calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the power transmitted (P) and the shaft rotation speed (N) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Shaft size calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns torque (T) (Power and torque), derived from the power transmitted (P) and the shaft rotation speed (N). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Shaft size calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the power transmitted (P) and the shaft rotation speed (N), which is 36 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter power transmitted (P) (Power and torque) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Power transmitted (P) (Power and torque) opens in kilowatts and the chip beside it offers 21 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Torque (T) = 9.5493 N·m. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Shaft size calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
